pending_items.title: Egypt's terror list targeting European Muslims echoes Israel and the UAE
pending_items.content:
In September, Egyptian police arrested all six journalists at Matsadaash, a news platform dedicated to fact-checking and investigative reporting. They were accused of spreading misinformation on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, a charge the outlet denies.

The authorities then turned on Mada Masr, one of Egypt's best-known independent news sites . In October, a court ordered the site closed. The following month, its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, faced a retrial on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The same charges brought her a one-year prison sentence in absentia in 2024.

Shaher Ayyad, an editorial board member at the news site al-Manassa, told Reuters : "Independent outlets are often portrayed as lawbreakers or enemies of the state."

Both cases are part of the repression that Amnesty International detailed in its 2025 report , which found that authorities "continued to criminalize dissenting forms of expression and peaceful assembly, targeting journalists, protesters, opposition politicians and others who criticized the government's human rights record or called for political change".

Egypt's record of abuse at home has long been documented. A decade after the former military chief took power , the US State Department's 2024 human rights report called the situation dire.

The department cited credible reports of "torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment; arbitrary arrest and detention", "instances of transnational repression against individuals in another country" and "serious restrictions on freedom of expression and media freedom, including unjustified arrests or prosecutions of journalists and censorship".

The list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions

On 10 November, Egypt went a step further and published a list of 35 associations and 36 individuals that the Cairo Criminal Court has designated as "terrorists".

Strikingly, the list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions, the national, cultural, educational and religious bodies that serve Muslim communities across 27 countries.

At its centre is the Council of European Muslims, formerly the Federation of Islamic Organisations in Europe, an umbrella body founded in 1989 whose members help Muslims practise their faith, preserve their identity and integrate into their societies.

The designations are valid for five years, subject to appeal, extension and removal. They were published just days after Egyptian authorities placed the Muslim Brotherhood permanently on the country's terrorism list, replacing a series of time-limited designations.

For those named, the practical consequences could include restrictions on travel and banking , and a real threat to their personal security .

Egypt's latest move has raised fears that it is exporting its crackdown on political dissent and extending its hunt for the Muslim Brotherhood, the movement that won the country's election in 2012 before being ousted the following year by the then defence minister, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

Anas Altikriti, the British-Iraqi founder of the Cordoba Foundation and one of the 36 individuals named, said Arab governments regard the political influence of Muslim communities in the West as a threat. "What you actually do is to shut down Muslim civil society in the West," he told The New Arab.

In 2014, three years after the Arab Spring uprisings, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates , among others, also designated the Brotherhood a "terrorist organisation".

The list was also published a month after the European Parliament's largest group, the European People's Party, pushed through a non-binding resolution "on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network".

The resolution had support from fellow conservatives, the far right and liberals, and opposition from the social democrats, the Greens and the left.

It explicitly named the Council of European Muslims, along with other Muslim and anti-racist organisations , and called for groups associated with the council to be denied access to EU institutions and removed from the EU's transparency register.

Amnesty International and more than 100 other civil society groups wrote to European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in protest, but the letter has gone unanswered.

Given that those targeted are based in Europe, there is reason to suspect a concerted effort by political forces seeking to criminalise Muslim and anti-racist civic life. The picture, however, is bigger than that.

It is a mistake to treat Cairo's terror list as a purely domestic decision, or even a Euro-Arab one. Egypt is better understood as part of a wider geopolitical strategy, the culmination of developments well beyond its borders.

First, Egypt has long wanted the Muslim Brotherhood on western terrorist lists, and some argue Sisi is acting largely on behalf of one of Egypt's main financiers , the UAE.

Second, it is no coincidence that those efforts gained ground under the second Trump administration . In November 2025, the president set in motion the designation of Brotherhood chapters, including Egypt's, as terrorist organisations by executive order rather than legislation.

That gave the Egyptian president the symbolic backing to keep telling a story that looks domestic at first glance.

The UAE, for its part, listed 15 civil society groups in the US and Europe as terrorist organisations in 2014, alongside armed groups such as al-Qaeda, Boko Haram and the Islamic State group.

They included the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights group in the US, and the forerunner of the Council of European Muslims, along with the national associations in France , Britain , Germany and Belgium that Cairo has now designated.

Muslim Brotherhood allegations are not a new invention, and they played a major role in November's US midterms , where they were levelled at Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed .

In January 2025, the UAE added eight companies registered in the UK and owned by Emirati dissidents and their relatives.

In February 2026, nine months before Egypt published its list, the Netanyahu government's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism released a report titled "The Muslim Brotherhood Across Europe".

The ministry makes no secret of its purpose. Its report says the ministry "systematically documents activities by those engaged in delegitimization" of Israel, and lists "cooperation with pro-Palestinian organizations" and the promotion of boycotts, sanctions and divestment among its areas of focus.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence

Its research department identified nine "key organizations in Europe".

Three of them appear among the eight Europe-wide associations on the Egyptian court's list: the Council of European Muslims, the European Council for Fatwa and Research, and the European Institute of Human Sciences. The Council of European Muslims is the first organisation named in both documents.

The Israeli ministry's report presents the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium as part of the Brotherhood's European network, and all four are now on Egypt's list. Nearly a third of the 36 individuals the Egyptian court named also appear in the report, including four men it identifies as presidents of the council.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence. It suggests Cairo is working from a script written elsewhere, further reducing the country that once led the Arab world to the role of a vessel for wealthy backers aligned with Israel.

pending_items.content:
By Muayad Hameed, Tala Ramadan and Maha El Dahan

BAGHDAD, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Iraq's prime minister has ordered the energy ministry to manage oilfields under the control of the Kurds, in a move likely to further strain relations with their semi-autonomous region after he sought to rein in an influential pro-Iranian militia.

The decision comes as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi cracks down on Tehran's most powerful militia ally in Iraq, Kataib Hezbollah, and senior officials accused of running a years-long smuggling ring that generated hundreds of millions of dollars from stolen oil.

Heavily armedKataib, one of dozens of pro-Iranian armed groups with political sway accused of operating with impunity in Iraq, rejected the findings of an official high-level investigation into the smuggling network.

The prime minister of the Kurdish region, Masrour Barzani, rejected the Baghdad government's decisions to centralise control over oil and border crossings, saying they "are in no way acceptable".

Zaidi's order, which was announced by his office on Tuesday, covers oilfields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces and follows a probe into smuggling at state-run North Oil Company, which manages the northern oil and gas fields.

Khormala, the main oilfield under Kurdish security control, appeared to be covered by the order, three people familiar with the matter said. Given past tensions with Baghdad, one of them said Kurdish authorities would likely resist any move by the federal oil ministry to take over management of the field.

"The Kurdistan region may use the absence of an oil and gas law as a pretext for refusing to hand over the oil wells. This would lead to a political and constitutional debate over how to implement the decisions," said Baghdad-based political analyst Hamza Mustafa.

"In taking these decisions, he has moved away from political deal-making and favouritism. He is unconcerned about securing the support of those political forces for another term. That is why he is taking on all the corruption networks."

A statement from his office said the prime minister's directive was based on the principle that "national sovereignty is indivisible and protecting Iraq's wealth is a battle for survival in which the state puts an end to all forms of smuggling."

PM CRACKS DOWN ON KURDISH SMUGGLING, IRAN ALLIES

In a further move directly challenging Kurdish authorities' decades-long bid to run their own affairs, Zaidi ordered the border authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdistan region, which borders Turkey, Iran and Syria. He also directed the Kurdistan Regional Government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal oil ministry.

Zaidi, meanwhile, removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company's director general and his deputies pending further investigation.

Relations between the national government and Kurdish authorities have been fraught for years.

Iraq's Kurds held a 2017 referendum on independence, which elicited fierce opposition from Baghdad and regional powers. The vote prompted military and economic retaliation from Baghdad, which retook the strategic oil-producing city ofKirkuk and other areas.

A previous dispute over Kurdish authorities' sales of oil without Baghdad's approval halted pipeline shipments to Turkey for more than two years before the sides agreed in September 2025 to restart them.

Zaidi — a multimillionaire businessman and political novice — is trying to attract large-scale investment in Iraq. Analysts, however, say that first requires establishing the political and economic stability that has been lacking since a 2003 US-led invasion toppled Saddam Hussein.

The upheaval — including pro-Saddam and al Qaeda insurgencies, a sectarian civil war and economic ruin — and strong ties with militias and prominent Shi'ite politicians who support them,has allowed Iran to steadily gain widespread influence in Iraq — an ally of both Washington and Tehran.

(Reporting by Tala Ramadan in Dubai and Muayad Hameed in Baghdad; Writing by Michael Georgy; Editing by Barbara Lewis and Joe Bavier)

pending_items.title: من الوقود إلى مائدة الطعام... كيف تؤثر توترات الشرق الأوسط على أسعار السلع في مصر؟
pending_items.content:
لم يعد تأثير أسعار الوقود في مصر مقتصرا على ما يدفعه أصحاب السيارات أو مستخدمو وسائل النقل.

فكل زيادة في تكلفة نقل البضائع من المزارع والمصانع إلى الأسواق، يمكن أن تنعكس على أسعار السلع، ولو بدرجات متفاوتة.

ومع استمرار التوترات الإقليمية وما يصاحبها من تقلبات في أسواق الطاقة وحركة الشحن، أصبحت تكلفة توفير الاحتياجات اليومية مصدر قلق لأسر تحاول التوفيق بين دخلها المالي ومصاريفها اليومية.

تتداخل في تحديد الأسعار عوامل محلية وخارجية، أبرزها سعر الصرف وتكاليف الإنتاج والاستيراد، والضرائب، وحجم العرض والطلب. لذلك لا يمكن ربط كل الزيادات في الأسعار بالأحداث الإقليمية وحدها. لكن اضطراب طرق التجارة أو ارتفاع أسعار النفط والتأمين والشحن يضيف أعباء جديدة، خصوصا على السلع التي تعتمد على مواد خام مستوردة، أو تحتاج إلى نقل متكرر بين المحافظات.

في القاهرة، تبدأ حسابات بعض الأسر قبل موعد التسوق نفسه. فالأولوية لإيجار المسكن وفواتير الكهرباء والغاز والمواصلات وتكاليف المدارس. فيما يتم صرف ما تبقى من الأموال لشراء الطعام والاحتياجات المنزلية.

اقرأ أيضا ارتفاع التضخم وتراجع القدرة الشرائية للمصريين، هل من حل؟

ويقول محمد عبدالله، وهو رب أسرة يعيل زوجته وطفلين: "في السابق، كنا نشتري طلبات البيت ونترك جزءا من المرتب لأي ظرف. لكن اليوم، المرتب ينقسم من أول الشهر، وأي زيادة أخرى تضطرنا للتقليل من الاحتياجات الاساسية. حتى النزول إلى المتاجر يحتاج الي تقييم الحسابات والمصاريف ".

ويضيف محمد أنه صار يقارن بين أسعار أكثر من متجر، ويشتري ما يكفي أياما محدودة بدلا من تخزين بعض السلع للشهر كله. أما النفقات المفاجئة، مثل زيارة الطبيب، وتكلفة العلاج، أو إصلاح جهاز منزلي، فقد تدفع الأسرة إلى الاستدانة أو تأجيل التزامات أخرى.

ولا تعني هذه التغييرات بالضرورة تراجع استهلاك كل الأسر بالوتيرة نفسها. فالأثر يختلف بحسب مستوى الدخل وعدد أفراد الأسرة ومكان السكن، لكنه يكشف كيف يمكن لارتفاع تكلفة بند أساسي واحد أن يضغط على بنود أخرى لا تقل أهمية.

يُعد النقل جزءا من تكلفة معظم السلع المتداولة في الأسواق المصرية، سواء كانت منتجات زراعية تصل من المحافظات إلى أسواق الجملة، أو مواد غذائية مصنعة تُنقل إلى الموزعين ثم المحلات التجارية. وتؤثر أسعار السولار ومصاريف الصيانة والعمالة في حسابات النقل، إلى جانب تكلفة التخزين والتبريد بالنسبة إلى بعض المنتجات.

وعندما ترتفع هذه المصاريف، لا تنتقل الزيادة بالضرورة كاملة أو فورا إلى المستهلك. فقد يتحمل المورد جزءا منها، أو يخفض التاجر هامش ربحه، أو تتغير الأسعار عند وصول شحنة جديدة. ويتوقف ذلك على طبيعة السلعة والمنافسة وحجم الطلب والقدرة على تخزينها.

كما أن الاضطرابات في البحر الأحمر أو مسارات الملاحة الأخرى قد تدفع بعض شركات الشحن إلى تغيير خطوط سيرها، ما يزيد مدة الرحلات أو تكاليف التأمين والنقل. ولا تتساوى آثار هذه التطورات على جميع المنتجات، لكنها تبرز مدى ارتباط الأسعار داخل السوق المحلية بحركة التجارة خارج الحدود.

بالنسبة إلى تجار المواد الغذائية، لا يقتصر الأمر على ثمن البضاعة عند شرائها. فهناك مصاريف توصيل وتخزين وأجور وكهرباء، فضلا عن احتمال اختلاف أسعار الموردين من شحنة إلى أخرى. وفي المقابل، يواجه التاجر مستهلكا أكثر حذرا في الإنفاق، قد يتراجع عن الشراء إذا تجاوز السعر قدرته.

ويشرح جمال الدين، أحد تجار المواد الغذائية في القاهرة : "المشكلة ليست فقط في ارتفاع سعر البضائع. هناك تكاليف نقل وعمالة ومصاريف تشغيلية. وكل بند يؤثر على التكلفة. وفي ذات الوقت المستهلك غير قادر على تحمل أي زيادة في التكاليف، فنحاول أن نبيع بهامش ربح أقل حتى لا تتكدس البضائع لدينا ".

ويضيف جمال الدين: " إن بعض الزبائن يفضلون العبوات الصغيرة أو البدائل الأقل سعرا، فيما يطلب آخرون معرفة السعر قبل اتخاذ قرار الشراء. ويضيف أن صعوبة توقع تكلفة الشحنة التالية تجعل التخطيط للمخزون أكثر تعقيدا، خصوصا للأنشطة التجارية الصغيرة التي لا تملك سيولة كبيرة.

داخل محال البقالة بالأحياء السكنية، تظهر آثار الضغط على الميزانيات في تفاصيل صغيرة: شراء قطعة واحدة بدلا من عبوة كاملة، أو اختيار علامة تجارية أقل سعرا، أو تأجيل شراء منتج غير ضروري. وقد لا تبدو هذه التغييرات كبيرة في عملية بيع منفردة، لكنها تتراكم مع مرور الوقت.

ويقول حسن الديب، مالك بقالة في القاهرة: "هناك زبائن كانوا يشترون احتياجات الأسبوع مرة واحدة، أما الآن فيشترون احتياجاتهم كل يومين وحتى عملية الشراء تتم حسب المبالغ المتوفرة لديهم. وهناك زبائن كثر يسألون عن البضائع الأقل ثمنا، وهنالك منتجات كانت تباع بسرعة، أما الآن فهي مكدسة على رفوف المحل منذ فترة طويلة".

ويضيف محدثنا أن بعض الزبائن يطلبون تسجيل مشترياتهم لحين قبض الراتب، بينما يحاول هو شراء كميات تناسب حركة البيع الفعلية حتى لا تتجمد أمواله في بضاعة يصعب تصريفها. ومع ذلك، لا يمكن تعميم تجربة محل واحد على السوق المصرية كلها، إذ تختلف أنماط الاستهلاك بين المناطق والفئات الاجتماعية.

تراجع معدل التضخم لا يعني بالضرورة عودة الأسعار إلى مستوياتها السابقة. فالتضخم يقيس وتيرة تغير الأسعار، وعندما يتباطأ قد تظل السلع أغلى مما كانت عليه قبل عام أو عامين، لكنها ترتفع بسرعة أقل. وهذا الفارق يفسر جانبا من التباين بين قراءة المؤشرات الاقتصادية وشعور المستهلك عند دفع فاتورة المشتريات.

وتختلف كذلك سلة الإنفاق من أسرة إلى أخرى. فالأسرة التي تنفق نسبة كبيرة من دخلها على الغذاء والنقل والسكن قد تشعر بضغط أكبر إذا ارتفعت أسعار هذه المواد، حتى إن تباطأ المؤشر العام. كما أن تحسن القدرة الشرائية لا يرتبط بالأسعار وحدها، بل بحركة الأجور والدخل، مقارنة بتكاليف المعيشة.

وتظل مصر معرضة لتقلبات الاقتصاد الإقليمي والعالمي بحكم ارتباطها بأسواق الطاقة والتجارة الدولية. لكن حجم التأثير يختلف بحسب مدة الاضطراب وطبيعته واستجابة الأسواق والسياسات المحلية. فالارتفاع المؤقت في تكلفة الشحن قد تكون له نتائج مختلفة عن اضطراب طويل الأمد في الإمدادات أو أسعار الوقود.

وفي الحياة اليومية، لا يتعامل المستهلك مع هذه العوامل بوصفها مؤشرات منفصلة، بل يراها مجتمعة في إجمالي ما يدفعه عند نهاية الشهر. وبين رب أسرة يعيد توزيع راتبه، وتاجر يحاول ضبط هامش الربح، وصاحب بقالة يراقب تغير مشتريات زبائنه، يظهر أن استقرار المؤشرات وحده لا يكفي لقياس تحسن الأوضاع المعيشية.

pending_items.title: Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
pending_items.content:
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the US-Israel war, including the missile attack on a school that killed at least 178 people, most of them schoolgirls.

Vice President for Legal Affairs Majid Ansari said on Sunday that Iran has begun legal proceedings in courts in the US and four European countries over “war crimes”, months after the deadly attack on a primary school in Minab in February on the first day of the ongoing war .

The lawsuits will cover the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei , Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported. They will also address the deaths of scientists, military commanders and civilians, as well as attacks on civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, ambulances and emergency facilities.

Speaking at a ceremony honouring the families of children killed in US and Israeli attacks, Ansari said his office is working with the country’s justice and foreign ministries to pursue claims under international law.

The courts in the US and European countries have not been identified, but Ansari said proceedings had been initiated in courts that accepted jurisdiction over the cases. He gave no further specific details.

Experts say the cases in Europe may offer a more viable legal avenue, while proceedings in the US face significant jurisdictional hurdles. But whether Iran can turn these proceedings into meaningful accountability is questionable.

“Iran is pursuing the legal avenues available to it, seeking accountability and preserving evidence,” Saeed Bagheri, an assistant professor in international law at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera.

“Compensation may be an objective, but it is far from assured.”

Iran is pursuing its cases in the US and Europe because it has limited access to international courts.

Ansari said Iran was considering filing a case with the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals charged with the most grave crimes. But Tehran – alongside the US and Israel – is not a signatory to the Rome Statute under which the court was formed in 2002. Iran would, therefore, need an independent basis for jurisdiction, such as a UN Security Council referral.

At the International Court of Justice (ICJ) – the world’s top court that handles legal disputes between states – jurisdiction depends on state consent under Article 36 of the ICJ, said Bagheri.

“Iran cannot simply demand a hearing in either court,” said the expert, who is also a fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law based in Germany.

Amid the legal hurdles, Iran has filed a number of cases in both domestic and international courts accusing the US and Israel of committing war crimes in the June 2025 war as well as the ongoing war. Iran says more than 3,500 people have been killed and 26,500 wounded in the war, along with widespread damage to civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, bridges and energy facilities.

In March, Iran filed a complaint at the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague, accusing Washington of military aggression, illegal economic sanctions and threats of force. The Tribunal was formed following the 1981 Algiers Accords brokered by Algeria.

On Sunday, Ansari said preparations were under way for a second complaint to the Tribunal over the current war.

In September, Iran’s judiciary issued indictments against 159 senior US and Israeli political and military officials over the assassination of Khamenei and military commanders, judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said.

The Iranian judiciary has also said that about 400 cases have been filed with Iranian courts as part of domestic and international legal proceedings, including one involving 350,000 plaintiffs, Press TV reported.

A judiciary official on Monday said that local courts have demanded $290bn in damages from the United States.

A separate civil lawsuit was filed in the US in September by the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC), a US civil society organisation, alongside several Iranian plaintiffs, including the father of a girl killed in the Minab school bombing. The case seeks a ruling that the US military campaign in Iran was unconstitutional. This case was not brought by the Iranian government.

The Minab school bombing is a large component of Iran’s pursuit of justice in the US and European courts.

In September, a report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found that the United States likely committed “war crimes” when it struck the school.

But Iran’s arsenal of evidence to prove that the Minab school bombing was a war crime would have to be wide in scope – civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish a war crime, said Bagheri in Reading.

Iran would need to establish who carried out the attack, what was targeted and what the relevant decision-makers knew at the time, he explained.

Calling a strike accidental also does not settle whether it was lawful or not, said Bagheri.

Investigators must assess whether the military followed the rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians, he added.

“For Minab, the crucial evidence would include targeting files, intelligence assessments, no-strike lists, collateral-damage estimates and records showing when the information was last verified,” Bagheri explained.

According to the UN Mission’s report, the civilian nature of the school was apparent and the US failed in its obligation “to do everything feasible” to verify that it was a military objective.

The report’s authors said that photographs and videos depicting the school before and after the attack showed “readily identifiable features” that it was associated with an educational facility for young children.

“According to public reporting, satellite imagery of the school before the strike also appears to show human figures, readily identifiable as children, gathered in its courtyard,” the report said.

Ultimately, the biggest challenge, said Bagheri, would be linking the evidence of what happened to the decisions, knowledge and intentions of specific military commanders or officials, rather than simply establishing that civilians were killed.

In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident, for which the Pentagon has not yet published any findings.

The Pentagon launched an internal investigation, but it has not yet publicly released its report.

Both the US and Israeli states, as well as individual officials and military commanders, could potentially be held responsible for the alleged violations, but under different legal frameworks.

State responsibility depends on whether an action can be attributed to a state and whether it breached international law, said Bagheri.

Individual criminal responsibility, meanwhile, can extend to those who carried out, ordered or assisted crimes, as well as commanders who failed to prevent or respond to crimes by forces under their effective control, the expert said.

Rank alone does not matter and investigators must establish what individuals knew, what authority they exercised and what they could have done, said Bagheri.

Still, immunity may also shield some officials from prosecution in foreign courts, particularly serving heads of state, government leaders and foreign ministers.

“Functional immunity for other officials accused of international crimes is more contested and depends on the forum,” said the expert from the University of Reading.

“But I would treat Khamenei’s killing separately. Article 110 of Iran’s Constitution gives the supreme leader command authority, but that title alone does not settle whether he was lawfully targetable.”

His actual military role and the circumstances of the attack matter, he added.

Iran may have a more viable path to pursuing its cases in Europe than in the US.

In some European countries, prosecutors can pursue serious international crimes under universal jurisdiction, regardless of the nationality of the accused or where the alleged offences happened.

But, Bagheri stressed, this route could lead to the prosecution of individuals – not a criminal trial of the US or Israeli governments.

The majority of European Union member states practice universal jurisdiction, according to the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust). The principle of universal jurisdiction allows the prosecution of individuals suspected of international crimes regardless of where they are committed.

In recent years, EU member states have been successful in bringing a number of perpetrators of international crimes to court on the basis of universal or extraterritorial jurisdiction, with convictions obtained in situations as diverse as Syria, Afghanistan, Rwanda and Liberia, including for crimes dating back 40 years, reports Eurojust.

Still, EU countries have varying requirements to proceed with a case, spanning their own presence, residence, nationality or territorial requirements, said Bagheri.

In his view, victims or civil parties are more likely to find success in producing investigations and preserving evidence than bringing senior US or Israeli officials to trial.

In the US, however, Iran faces “serious obstacles” in pursuing its cases, Bagheri said.

pending_items.title: China walks ‘thin line’ in push to prevent another Horn of Africa war
pending_items.content:
Beijing, China – China has stepped up diplomatic efforts in the Horn of Africa, sending senior envoys to four countries to ease mounting tensions that threaten to plunge the region into another devastating conflict.

Beijing’s special representative for African affairs, Liu Xianfa, travelled to Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early November, while its special envoy for Horn of Africa affairs, Hu Changchun, visited Eritrea. They met senior officials, including Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and the foreign ministers of Ethiopia and Egypt.

Announcing the visits on November 2, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said they were aimed at “promoting talks for peace, easing tensions, and playing a constructive role for upholding regional peace and stability”.

The visits followed a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, raising fears of another war between the neighbours. Meanwhile, longstanding disputes involving Egypt threaten to draw other countries into a wider confrontation.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a devastating border war between 1998 and 2000, killing tens of thousands of people. A historic peace agreement in 2018 ended two decades of hostility, but their reconciliation began to unravel following Ethiopia’s civil war in the northern Tigray region.

Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian government troops against Tigrayan fighters, but Eritrea was excluded from the 2022 peace agreement that ended the main phase of the war.

Central to their latest dispute is Ethiopia’s push to secure access to the Red Sea. The country has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993 and relies heavily on neighbouring Djibouti’s ports for international trade. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed argues access to the sea is essential for his country’s future, but his government’s interest in Eritrea’s strategic port of Assab has raised fears in Asmara over its territorial sovereignty.

Both governments accuse each other of supporting armed groups.

Complicating matters is Ethiopia’s longstanding dispute with Egypt over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile. Cairo fears the project could threaten its water supply, while Addis Ababa insists it has the right to harness the river for electricity generation and economic development.

Egypt has strengthened its relationship with Eritrea, adding another dimension to the growing tensions. Recent reports of Ethiopian and Eritrean troops gathering near their shared border have heightened fears of a wider conflict.

China has billions of dollars at stake in the Horn of Africa, which sits along one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes. Between 2000 and 2023, China committed $17.8bn in loans to Ethiopia, according to United States-based research institute AidData.

Edson Ziso, a visiting research fellow at the University of Adelaide, says China has played a “starring role” in Ethiopia’s economic transformation. Among Beijing’s flagship infrastructure projects is the $4.3bn Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, which connects landlocked Ethiopia to the coast.

Meanwhile, Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military base, which opened in 2017. The country sits near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a crucial shipping passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. “The Strait of Hormuz stalemate has already highlighted the huge cost conflict can inflict on the global economy when vital shipping lanes are choked,” says Ziso.

China’s efforts also reflect President Xi Jinping’s desire to portray his country as a major diplomatic player and contributor to global peace and stability, say analysts. Beijing has promoted what it calls the “Outlook on Peace and Development in the Horn of Africa”, a 2022 framework that emphasises African-led solutions to security challenges.

Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow with the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, says Beijing’s approach is focused on helping countries in the region “control their security destiny”, rather than imposing solutions from outside. She says Beijing’s view is that “development gaps fuel instability,” but success depends on all parties accepting that “confrontation leaves all of them worse off.”

China’s close relationships with governments across the region put it in a position to encourage dialogue, but its ability to broker meaningful compromises remains unclear.

Beijing’s principle of noninterference has helped it cultivate relationships across Africa. Yet the disputes involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt concern deeply sensitive questions of territory, sovereignty and water security. Economic incentives may not be enough to resolve them, caution analysts.

Among the obstacles, Khan says, are actors outside the region who have “stoked confrontation and disrupted African-led processes”. Ziso says the involvement of proxy forces, fighter groups and rebels also presents a significant challenge.

And while all regional countries have close ties with Beijing, some, particularly Egypt, have longstanding security relationships with Washington. Ziso says this could limit China’s ability to achieve a breakthrough if governments perceive Chinese-led solutions as jeopardising relations with the US.

Against that backdrop, China’s recent diplomatic visits have produced statements of support for greater cooperation and regional peace, but no formal negotiations or concrete agreements have been announced.

“China is thus walking a thin line,” Ziso says, adding that all four countries – Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti – are critical to Beijing’s economic and strategic interests. “China may need to look beyond its own interests in pursuit of concrete and sustainable de-escalation.”
